Thus the community of <hi type="italic">el-Hîgâne</hi>, ten years since, had compacts with 101 tribes; and that Job also did this, seems evident from the fact that the poet represents him as surprised not by neighbouring, but by far distant tribes (Chaldaeans and Sabaeans), with whom he could have no compact.<note placement="foot">These sudden attacks, at any rate, do not say anything in favour of the more southernly position of <hi type="italic">Ausitis</hi>. If the Beduin is but once on his horse or <hi type="italic">delûl</hi>, it is all the same to him whether a journey is ten days longer or shorter, if he can only find water for himself and his beast. This, however, both bands of marauders found, since the poet distinctly represents the attacks as having been made in the winter. The general ploughing of the fallow-lying <hi type="italic">wâgiha</hi> of a community (it is called <hi type="italic">shiqâq el - wâgiha</hi>), ready for the sowing in the following autumn, always takes place during January and February, because at this time of the year the earth is softened by the winter rains, and easy to plough. While engaged in this work, the poet represents Job’s ploughmen as being surprised and slain. Hence, for the destruction of 500 armed ploughmen - and they were armed, because they could only have been slain with their weapons in their hands in consequence of their resistance - at least 2000 horsemen were necessary. So large a <hi type="italic">ghazwe</hi> is, however, not possible in the summer, but only in the winter, because they could not water at a draw-well, only at the pools (<hi type="italic">ghudrân</hi>) formed by the winter rains. For one of these raids of the Chaldaeans, <hi type="italic">Haurân</hi>, whither marauding bands come even now during the winter from the neighbourhood of Babylon in six or seven days, lay far more convenient than the country around <hi type="italic">Ma'ân</hi> and <hi type="italic">'Akaba</hi>, which is only reached from the Euphrates, even in winter, by going a long way round, since the <hi type="italic">Nufûd</hi> (sandy plains) in the east, and their western continuation the <hi type="italic">Hâlât</hi>, suck in the rain without forming any pools. On the other hand, however, this southern region lay nearer and more convenient for the incursions of the Sabaeans, viz., the Keturaean (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.3">Gen 25:3</reference>), i.e., Petraean tribe of this name. The greater or less distance, however, is of little consequence here. Thus, as the <hi type="italic">Shemmar</hi> of <hi type="italic">Negd</hi> from time to time make raids into the neighbourhood of Damascus, so even the tribes of <hi type="italic">Wâdi el-Korâ</hi> might also do the same. Moreover, as we observed above, the poet represents the sudden attacks as perpetrated by the Sabaeans and Chaldaeans, probably because <hi type="italic">they only</hi>, as being foreign and distant races which never had anything to do with Job and his men, and therefore were without any consideration, could practise such unwonted barbarities as the robbery of ploughing heifers, which a <hi type="italic">ghazwe</hi> rarely takes, and the murder of the ploughmen.</note> <div eID="gen8866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8867" type="x-p"/> Next he proceeds to erect a <hi type="italic">chirbe</hi>, i.e., a village that has been forsaken (for a longer or shorter period), in connection with which, excepting the relations, slaves, and servants of the master, all those whom interest, their calling, and confidence in the good fortune of the master, have drawn thither, set about the work. Perhaps <reference osisRef="Job.15.28">Job 15:28</reference> has reference to Job’s settlement.<note placement="foot">Verbally, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.3.14">Job 3:14</reference></hi>, which we, however, have interpreted differently, accords with this. - Del.</note> <div eID="gen8867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8868" type="x-p"/> With reference to the relation of the lord of a village (<hi type="italic">ustâd beled ,</hi> or <hi type="italic">sâhib dê‛a</hi>) to his work-people, there are among the dependents two classes. The one is called <hi type="italic">zurrâ‛</hi>, “sowers,” also <hi type="italic">fellâhin kism</hi>, “participating husbandmen,” because they share the produce of the harvest with the <hi type="italic">ustâd</hi> thus: he receives a fourth while they retain three-fourths, from which they live, take the seed for the following season, give their quota towards the demands of the Arabs, the village shepherds, the field watchmen, and the scribe of the community (<hi type="italic">chatı̂b</hi>); they have also to provide the farming implements and the yoke-oxen. On the other hand, the <hi type="italic">ustâd</hi> has to provide for the dwellings of the people, to pay the land-tax to the government, and, in the event of a failure of the crops, murrain, etc., to make the necessary advances, either in money or in kind at the market price, and without any compensation. This relation, which guarantees the maintenance of the family, and is according to the practice of a patriarchal equity, is greatly esteemed in the country; and one might unhesitatingly consider it therefore to be that which existed between Job and his ploughmen, because it may with ease exist between a single <hi type="italic">ustâd</hi> and hundreds, indeed thousands, of country people, if <reference osisRef="Job.1.3">Job 1:3</reference> did not necessitate our thinking of another class of country people, viz., the <hi type="italic">murâbi‛ı̂n</hi>, the “quarterers.” They take their name from their receiving a fourth part of the harvest for their labour, while they have to give up the other three-fourths to the <hi type="italic">ustâd</hi>, who must provide for their shelter and board, and in like manner everything that is required in agriculture. As Job, according to <reference osisRef="Job.1.3">Job 1:3</reference> (comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.42.12">Job 42:12</reference>), provided the yoke-oxen and means of transport (asses and camels), so he also provided the farming implements, and the seed for sowing. We must not here think of the paid day-labourer of the Syrian towns, or the servants of our landed proprietors; they are unknown on the borders of the desert. The hand that toils has there a direct share in the gain; the workers belong to the <hi type="italic">aulâd</hi>, “children of the house,” and are so called; in the hour of danger they will risk their life for their lord. <div eID="gen8868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8869" type="x-p"/> This rustic labour is always undertaken simultaneously by all the <hi type="italic">murâbi‛ı̂n</hi> (it is so also in the villages of the <hi type="italic">zurrâ‛</hi>) for the sake of order, since the <hi type="italic">ustâd</hi>, or in his absence the village sheikh, has the general work of the following day announced from the roof of his house every evening. Thus it is explained how the 500 ploughmen could be together in one and the same district, and be slain all together. <div eID="gen8869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8870" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">ustâd</hi> is the sole judge, or, by deputy, the <hi type="italic">sheikh</hi>. An appeal to the government of the country would be useless, because it has no influence in Hauran; but the servant who has been treated unjustly by his master, very frequently turns as <hi type="italic">dachı̂l fi 'l - haqq</hi> (a suppliant concerning his right) to his powerful neighbour, who is bound, according to the customs of the country, to obtain redress for him (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.29.12-Job.29.17">Job 29:12-17</reference>). If he does not obtain this by persuasion, he cries for force, and such a demand lies at the root of many a bloody feud. <div eID="gen8870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8871" type="x-p"/> Powerful and respected also as the position, described in <reference osisRef="Job.29.1">Job 29:1</reference>, of such a man is, it must, according to the nature of its basis, fall in under strokes of misfortune, like those mentioned in <reference osisRef="Job.1.14-Job.1.19">Job 1:14-19</reference>, and change to the very opposite, as the poet describes it in Job 30:1. <div eID="gen8871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8872" type="x-p"/> After these observations concerning the agricultural relations of Hauran, we return to the tradition of Job. As we pursue the track of this tradition further, we first find it again in some of the Christina writers of the middle ages, viz., in Eugesippus (<hi type="italic">De distanc. loc. terr. sanct.</hi>), in William of Tyre (<hi type="italic">Histor. rerum a Francis gest.</hi>), and in Marino Sanuto (<hi type="italic">De secretis fid. cruc.</hi>). The passages that bear upon the point are brought together in Reland (<hi type="italic">Palest</hi>. pp. 265f.); and we would simply refer to them, if it were possible for the reader to find his way among the fabulous confusion of the localities in Eugesippus and Sanuto. <div eID="gen8872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8873" type="x-p"/> The oldest of these citations is from Eugesippus, and is as follows: One part of the country is the land of <hi type="italic">Hus</hi>, out of which Job was; it is also called <hi type="italic">Sueta</hi>, after which Bildad the Suhite was named. Sanuto tells us where this locality is to be sought. “<hi type="italic">Sueta</hi> is the home of Baldad the Suite, Below this city (<hi type="italic">civitas</hi>), in the direction of the Kedar-tribes, the Saracens are accustomed to assemble out of Aram, Mesopotamia, Ammon, Moab, and the whole Orient, around the fountain of <hi type="italic">Fiale;</hi> and, on account of the charms of the place, to hold a fair there during the whole summer, and to pitch their coloured tents.” In another place he says: <hi type="italic">fontem Fialen Medan,</hi> i.e., <hi type="italic">aquas Dan, a Saracenis nuncupari.</hi> <div eID="gen8873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8874" type="x-p"/> Now, since according to an erroneous, but previously prevalent etymology, “the water of Dan” (מי דן = יאר דּן) denoted the Jordan, and since we further know from Josephus (<hi type="italic">Bell</hi>. iii. 10, 7) that the <hi type="italic">Phiala</hi> is the small lake of <hi type="italic">Râm</hi>, whose subterranean outflow the tetrarch Philip is said to have shown to be the spring of the Jordan, which comes to light deeper below, we should have thought the country round about the lake of Râm, at the south foot of Hermôn, to be the home of Job and Bildad. This discovery would be confirmed by the following statement of Eugesippus (in Reland, <hi type="italic">loc. cit.</hi>): “The river <hi type="italic">Dan</hi> flows under ground from its spring as far as the plain of Meldan, where it comes to light. This plain is named after the fair, which is held there, for the Saracens call such an one <hi type="italic">Meldan</hi>. At the beginning of the summer a large number of men, with wares to sell, congregate there, and several Parthian and Arabian soldiers also, in order to guard the people and their herds, which have a rich pasture there in the summer. The word <hi type="italic">Meldan</hi> is composed of <hi type="italic">mel</hi> and <hi type="italic">dan</hi>.” It is indeed readily seen that the writer has ignorantly jumbled several words together in the expression <hi type="italic">meldan</hi>, as <hi type="italic">mê Dan</hi>, “water of Dan,” and <hi type="italic">Mêdân</hi> or <hi type="italic">mı̂dân</hi>, “market-place;” perhaps even also <hi type="italic">leddân</hi>, the name of the great fountain of the Jordan in the crater of the <hi type="italic">Tell el-Kâdi</hi>. In like manner, the statement that the neighbourhood of <hi type="italic">Phiala</hi>, or that of the large fountain of the Jordan, might formerly have been a fair of the tribes, is false, for the former is broken up into innumerable craters, and the latter is poisoned by the swamp-fevers of the <hi type="italic">Hûle;</hi> but as to the rest, both Eugesippus and Sanuto seem really to speak of a tradition which places Job’s or Bildad’s home in that region. And yet it is not so: their tradition is no other than the Hauranitish; but ignorance of the language and geography of the country, and some accidental circumstances, so confused their representations, that it is difficult to find out what is right. The first clue is given us by the history of William of Tyre, in which (l. xxii. c. 21) it is said that the crusaders, on their return from a marauding expedition in the Nukra, wished to reconquer a strong position, the <hi type="italic">Cavea Roob,</hi> which they had lost a short time before. “This place,” says the historian, “lies in the province of <hi type="italic">Suite</hi>, a district distinguished by its pleasantness, etc.; and that Baldad, Job’s friend, who is on that account called the Suite, is said to have come from it.” This passage removes us at once into the neighbourhood of <hi type="italic">Muzêrîb</hi> and the Monastery of Job, for the province of Suete is nothing but the district of <hi type="italic">Suwêt</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣwı̂t</hi>),<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Reisebericht</hi>, S. 46; comp. Ritter, <hi type="italic">Syr. u. Pal.</hi> ii. 1019 [<hi type="italic">Erdk</hi>. xv. Pt. 2, p. 1019].</note> the north-western boundary of which is formed by the gorge of the <hi type="italic">Wâdî Rahûb</hi>. The Cavea Roob, which was first of all again found out by me on my journey in 1862, lies in the middle of the steep bank of that wadi, and is at present called <hi type="italic">maghâret Rahûb</hi>, “the cave of R.,” or more commonly <hi type="italic">mu'allakat Rahûb</hi>, “the swinging cave of R.,” and at the time of the Crusades commanded the dangerous pass which the traveller, on ascending from the south end of the Lake of Galilee to <hi type="italic">Edre'ât</hi> by the nearest way, has to climb on hands and feet. In another passage (xvi. 9), where the unhealthy march to <hi type="italic">Bosrâ</hi> is spoken of, Will. of Tyre says: “After we had come through the gorge of <hi type="italic">Roob</hi>, we reached the plain which is called <hi type="italic">Medan</hi>, and where every year the Arabs and other oriental tribes are accustomed to hold a large fair.” This plain is in the vicinity of <hi type="italic">Muzêrîb</hi>, in which the great pilgrim-fair is held annually. We find something similar in xiii. 18: “After having passed Decapolis<note placement="foot">Here in the more contracted sense, the district of <hi type="italic">Gadara, Kefârât,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Irbid</hi>.</note> we came to the pass of <hi type="italic">Roob</hi>, and further on into the plain of <hi type="italic">Medan</hi>, which stretches far and wide in every direction, and is intersected by the river <hi type="italic">Dan</hi>, which falls into the Jordan between (<hi type="italic">Tiberias</hi> and <hi type="italic">Scythopolis</hi> (<hi type="italic">Bîsân</hi>).” This river, the same as that which Sanuto means by his <hi type="italic">aquae Dan </hi>(<hi type="italic">Mê Dâ</hi>n), is none other than the <hi type="italic">Wâdi el-Meddân</hi>, called “the overflowing one,” because in the month of March it overflows its banks eastward of the <hi type="italic">Gezzâr</hi>-bridge. It is extremely strange that the name of this river appears corrupted not only in all three writers mentioned above, but also in Burckhardt; for, deceived by the ear, he calls it <hi type="italic">Wâdî Om el-Dhan</hi>.<note placement="foot">Burckhardt, <hi type="italic">Travels in Syr. and Pal</hi>. (ed. Gesenius, S. 392).</note> <div eID="gen8874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8875" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Meddân</hi> is the boundary river between the <hi type="italic">Suwêt</hi> and <hi type="italic">Nukra</hi> plains; it loses its name where it runs into the <hi type="italic">Makran;</hi> and where it falls into the valley of the Jordan, below the lake of Tiberias, it is called <hi type="italic">el-Muchêbî</hi>. <div eID="gen8875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8876" type="x-p"/> We have little to add to what has been already said. The <hi type="italic">Fiale</hi> of Sanuto is not the Lake Râm, but the round <hi type="italic">begge</hi>, the lake of springs of Muzêrîb, the rapid outflow of which, over a depth of sixty to eighty feet, forms a magnificent waterfall, the only one in Syria, as it falls into the Meddân near the village of <hi type="italic">Tell Shihâb</hi>. <div eID="gen8876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8877" type="x-p"/> The unfortunate confusion of the localities was occasioned by two accidental circumstances: first, that both the springs of the Jordan below <hi type="italic">Bâniâs</hi> and the lake of <hi type="italic">Muzêrîb</hi>, have a village called <hi type="italic">Rahûb</hi> (רחוב) in their vicinity, of which one is mentioned in Jdg 18:28., and the other, about a mile below the <hi type="italic">Cavea Roob</hi>, is situated by a fountain of the same name, from which village, cavern, and wadi derive their names; secondly, that there, as here, there is a village <hi type="italic">Abil</hi> (אבל): that near Dan is situated in the “meadow-district of 'Ijôn” (<hi type="italic">Merg. 'Ijûn</hi>); and that in the Suwêt lies between <hi type="italic">Rahûb</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Makran</hi>, and was visited by Seetzen as well as by myself. Perhaps the circumstance that, just as the environs of <hi type="italic">Muzêrîb</hi> have their <hi type="italic">Mîdân</hi>,<note placement="foot">The word <hi type="italic">el - mı̂dân</hi> and <hi type="italic">el - mêdân</hi> signifies originally the hippodrome, then the arena of the sham-fight, then the place of contest, the battle-field, and finally a wide level place where a large concourse of men are accustomed to meet. In this sense the Damascenes have their <hi type="italic">el - mı̂dân</hi>, the Spanish cities their <hi type="italic">almeidân</hi>, and the Italians their <hi type="italic">corso</hi>.</note> so the environs of <hi type="italic">Bâniâs</hi> have their <hi type="italic">Ard el-Mejâdîn</hi>, “region of battle-fields,” may also have contributed to the confusion; thus, for example, the country sloping to the west from the <hi type="italic">Phiala</hi> towards the <hi type="italic">Hûle</hi>, between <hi type="italic">Gubbâtâ ez-zêt</hi> and <hi type="italic">Za'ûra</hi>, is called, perhaps on account of the murderous encounters which took place there, both in the time of the Crusades and also in more ancient times. It is certainly the ground on which the battle narrated in the book of Joshua, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.1">Jos 11:1</reference>, took place, and also the battle in which Antiochus the Great slew the Egyptian army about 200 b.c.) <div eID="gen8877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8878" type="x-p"/> What we have gained for our special purpose from this information (by which not a few statements of Ritter, K. v. Raumer, and others, are substantiated), is not merely the fact that the tradition which places Job’s home in the region of <hi type="italic">Muzêrîb</hi> existed even in the middle ages (which the quotation given above from <hi type="italic">Makdeshî</hi>, who lived before the time of the Crusades, also confirms), and even came to the ears of the foreigners who settled in the country as they then passed through the land, but also the certainty that this tradition was then, as now, common to the Christians and the Mussulmans, for the three writers previously mentioned would hardly have recorded it on the testimony of the latter only.<note placement="foot">Estôri ha-Parchi, the most renowned Jewish topographer of Palestine, in his work <hi type="italic">Caftor wa-ferach</hi>, completed in 1322 (newly edited by Edelmann, published by Asher, Berlin, 1852, S. 49), says דאר איוב lies one hour south of נבו, since he identifies <hi type="italic">Nawâ</hi> with the Reubenitish <hi type="italic">Nebô</hi>, Num 32:38, as <hi type="italic">Zora''</hi> with יעזר, Num 32:35; so that he explains ארץ עוץ by ארץ יעזר, although he at the same time considers the name, according to Saadia, as one with אלגוטה (<hi type="italic">el Ghuta</hi>). His statements moreover are exact, as one might expect from a man who had travelled for seven years in all directions in Palestine; and his conclusion, ארץ עוץ היא ארץ קדם לארץ ישׂראל כנגד טבריא, perfectly accords with the above treatise. - Del.</note> <div eID="gen8878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8879" type="x-p"/> There can be no doubt as to which of these two religions must be regarded as the original mother of this tradition. The Hauranite Christians, who, from their costume, manners, language, and traditions, undoubtedly inherited the country from the pre-Muhammedan age, venerate the Makâm perhaps even more than the Muhammedans; which would be altogether impossible in connection with the hostile position of the two religious sects towards one another, and in connection with the zealous scorn with which the Syrian Christians regard the religion of Islam, if the Hauranitish tradition of Job and the Makâm were of later, Muhammedan origin. It is also possible that, on a closer examination of the Makâm and the buildings about the Sachra, one might find, besides crosses, Greek inscriptions (since they are nowhere wanting in the Nukra), which could only have their origin in the time before the occupation of Islam (635 a.d.); for <hi type="italic">after</hi> this the Hauranite Christians, who only prolong their existence by wandering from <hi type="italic">chirbe</hi> to <hi type="italic">chirbe</hi>, have not even built a single dwelling-house, much less a building for religious worship, which was forbidden under pain of death in the treaty of Omar. But in connection with the pre-Islam Monastery of Job, which owed its origin only to the sacred tradition that held its ground in that place, are monumental witnesses that this tradition is pre-Islamic, and has been transferred from the Christians to the Mussulmans, required? We may go even further, and assert that Muhammed, in the Sur. xxxviii. 41ff. of the <hi type="italic">Korân</hi>, had the Hauranitish tradition of Job and the localities near <hi type="italic">Sa'dîje</hi> definitely before his mind. <div eID="gen8879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8880" type="x-p"/> We must regard the merchandise caravans which the inhabitants of <hi type="italic">Tehâma</hi> sent continuously into the “north country,” <hi type="italic">esh - shâm</hi>,<note placement="foot">In Jemen the Higâz, Syria may have been called <hi type="italic">Shâm</hi> in the earliest times. The name was taken into Syria itself by the immigration of the Jemanic tribes of <hi type="italic">Kudâ'a</hi>, and others, because they brought with them the name of Syria that was commonly used in their native land.</note> and the return freight of which consisted chiefly of Hauranitish corn, as proof of a regular intercourse between the east Jordanic country and the west of the Arabian peninsula in the period between Christ and Muhammed. Hundreds of men from Mekka and Medina came every year to <hi type="italic">Bosrâ;</hi> indeed, when it has happened that the wandering tribes of Syria, which were, then also as now, bound for Hauran with the <hi type="italic">kêl</hi>, i.e., their want of corn, got before them, and had emptied the granaries of Bosrâ, or when the harvests of the south of Hauran had been destroyed by the locusts, which is not unfrequently the case, they will have come into the <hi type="italic">Nukra</hi><note placement="foot">The remarkable fair at <hi type="italic">Muzêrîb</hi> can be traced back to the earliest antiquity, although Bosrâ at times injured it; but this latter city, from its more exposed position, has been frequently laid in ruins. It is probable that the merchants of Damascus pitched their tents for their <hi type="italic">Kasaba</hi>, i.e., their moveable fair, twice a year (in spring and in autumn) by the picturesque lake of Muzêrîb. If, with the tradition, we take the <hi type="italic">Nukra</hi> to be the home of Job, of the different ways of interpreting <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">Job 6:19</reference> there is nothing to hinder our deciding upon that which considers it as the greater caravan which acme periodically out of southern Arabia to Hauran (Bosrâ or Muzêrib). <hi type="italic">Têmâ</hi> with its well, <hi type="italic">Heddâg</hi> (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.21.14">Isa 21:14</reference>), celebrated by the poets of the steppe, from which ninety camels (<hi type="italic">sâniât</hi>) by turns raise a constantly flowing stream of clear and cool water for irrigating the palms and the seed, was in ancient times, perhaps, the crossing point of the merchant caravans going from south to north, and from east to west. Even under the Omajad Cahlifs the Mekka pilgrim-route went exclusively by way of <hi type="italic">Têmâ</hi>, just as during the Crusades so long as the Franks kept possession of <hi type="italic">Kerak</hi> and <hi type="italic">Shôbak</hi>. An attempt made in my <hi type="italic">Reisebericht</hi> (S. 93-95) to substitute the Hauranitish <hi type="italic">Têmâ</hi> in the two previously mentioned passages of Scripture, I have there (S. 131) given up as being scarcely probable.</note> as far as Nawâ, sometimes even as far as Damascus, in order to obtain their full cargo. <div eID="gen8880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8881" type="x-p"/> If commerce often has the difficult task of bringing together the most heterogeneous peoples, and of effecting a reciprocal interchange of ideas, it here had the easy work of sustaining the intercourse among tribes that were originally one people, spoke one idiom, and regarded themselves as all related; for the second great Sabaean migration, under <hi type="italic">'Amr</hi> and his son <hi type="italic">Ta'labe</hi>, had taken possession of Mekka, and left one of their number, <hi type="italic">Rabî'a ibn Hâritha</hi>, with his attendants (the Chuzâ'ites), behind as lord of the city. In the same manner they had become possessed of <hi type="italic">Jathrib</hi> (<hi type="italic">el-Medîna</hi>), and left this city to their tribes <hi type="italic">Aus</hi> and <hi type="italic">Chazreg:</hi> the remainder of the people passed on to Peraea and took possession of the country, at that time devastated, as far as Damascus, according to <hi type="italic">Ibn Sa'îd</hi>, even including this city. By the reception of Christianity, the Syrian Sabaeans appear to have become but slightly or not at all estranged from their relatives in the Higâz, for Christianity spread even here, so that the Caesars once ventured to appoint a Christian governor even to the city of <hi type="italic">Mekka</hi>. This was during the lifetime of the Gefnite king <hi type="italic">'Amr ibn Gebele</hi>. At the time of Muhammed there were many Christians in Mekka, who will for the most part have brought their Christianity with the Syrian caravans, so that at the commencement of Islâm the Hauranitish tradition of Job might have been very well known in Mekka, since many men from Mekka may have even visited the Makâm and the Sachra, and there have heard many a legend of Job like that intimated in the Korân xxxviii. 43. Yea, whoever will give himself the trouble to investigate minute commentaries on the Koran, especially such as interpret the Koran from the tradition (<hi type="italic">hadı̂th</hi>), e.g., the <hi type="italic">Kitâb ed-durr el-muchtâr</hi>, may easily find that not merely <hi type="italic">Kazwînî, Ibn el-Wardî,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jâkût</hi>, whose observations concerning the Monastery of Job have been given above, but also much older authorities, identify the Koranish fountain of Job with the Hauranitish. <div eID="gen8881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8882" type="x-p"/> A statement of Eusebius, of value in connection with this investigation, brings us at one stride about three hundred years further on. It is in the <hi type="italic">Onomastikon</hi>, under Καρναείμ, and is as follows: “<hi type="italic">Astaroth Karnaim</hi> is at present (about 310 a.d.) a very large village (κώμη μεγίστη) beyond the Jordan, in the province of Arabia, which is also called <hi type="italic">Batanaea</hi>. Here, according to tradition (ἐκ παραδόσεως), they fix the dwelling (οἶκος) of Job.” On the small map which accompanies these pages, the reader will find in the vicinity of the Makâm the low and somewhat precipitous mound, not above forty feet in height, of <hi type="italic">Tell 'Ashtarâ</hi>, the plateau of which forms an almost round surface, which is 425 paces in diameter, and shows the unartistic foundations of buildings, and traces of a ring-wall. Here we have to imagine that <hi type="italic">'Astarot Karnaim</hi>. Euseb. here makes no mention whatever of the city of <hi type="italic">Astaroth</hi>, the ancient capital of <hi type="italic">Basan</hi>, for this he does under Astaroo'th; the hypothesis of its being the residence of king 'Og, which Newbold<note placement="foot">C. Ritter, <hi type="italic">Geogr. v. Syr. u. Pal.</hi> ii. 819ff. [<hi type="italic">Erdk</hi>. xv. 2, p. 819ff.] The information of Newbold, which is printed in the <hi type="italic">Zeitschr. d. Deutsch. Morgenl. Gesellschaft,</hi> i. 215f., is unfortunately little to be relied on, and is to be corrected according to the topography of the mound given above.</note> set up here, consequently falls to the ground. The κώμη μεγίστη of Eusebius must, in connection with the limited character of the ground, certainly be somewhat contracted; but the identity of the localities is not to be doubted in connection with the great nearness of the οἶκος (the Makâm).<note placement="foot">A small, desolated stone village, situated a quarter of an hour’s journey from the mound of <hi type="italic">'Ashtarâ</hi>, which however has not a single house of any importance, has two names among the inhabitants of that region, either <hi type="italic">Chirbêt 'Ijûn en-Nîle</hi> (the ruins near the Nila-springs) or <hi type="italic">Chirbêt 'Ashtarâ</hi>, which can signify the ruins of <hi type="italic">'Ashtarâ</hi> and the ruins near <hi type="italic">'Ashtarâ</hi>. Since it is, however, quite insignificant, it will not be the village that has given the name to the mound, but the mound with its buildings, which in ancient days were perhaps a temple to Astarte, surrounded by a wall, has given the name to the village.</note> <div eID="gen8882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8883" type="x-p"/> Let us compare another statement that belongs here; it stands under Ἀσταρὼθ Καρναείμ, and is as follows: “There are at the present time two villages of this name in Batanaea, which lie nine miles distant from one another, μεταξὺ ΑΔΑΡΩΝ καὶ ΑΒΙΛΗΞ.” Jerome has <hi type="italic">duo castella</hi> instead of two villages, by which at least the κώμη μεγίστη is somewhat reduced; for that it is one of these two castles<note placement="foot">The meaning of “castle,” as defined by Burckhardt, <hi type="italic">Travels in Syr.</hi> etc. p. 657, should be borne in mind here. “The name of <hi type="italic">Kal'at</hi> or <hi type="italic">castle</hi> is given on the Hadj route, and over the greater part of the desert, to any building walled in and covered, and having, like a <hi type="italic">Khan</hi>, a large courtyard in its enclosure. The walls are sometimes of stone, but more commonly of earth, though even the latter are sufficient to withstand an attack of Arabs.” - Tr.</note> can be the less doubtful, since they also regulate the determining of the respective localities. If the reading ΑΒΙΛΗΞ is correct, only <hi type="italic">Abil</hi> (אבל) in the north of Suwêt can (since, without doubt, the Arabian names of the places in Hauran existed in Eusebius’ day) be intended; and ΑΔΑΡΩΝ ought then to be changed into ΑΛΑΡΩΝ, in order to denote the large village of <hi type="italic">El-hârâ</hi>, on the lofty peak of the same name in the plain of Gêdûr. <hi type="italic">El-hârâ</hi> lies to the north, and <hi type="italic">Abil</hi> to the south of <hi type="italic">'Ashtarâ</hi>. If, however, as is most highly probable, instead of ΑΒΙΛΗΞ (which form Euseb. does not use elsewhere, for he calls the town of <hi type="italic">Abil</hi> Ἀβέλ, and the inscription in <hi type="italic">Turra</hi> has the form πόλεως Ἀβέλις), ΑΒΙΔΗΞ is to be read, which corresponds to the Ἀβιδᾶ of Ptolemy (<hi type="italic">ed. Wilberg</hi>, p. 369) and the modern /<hi type="italic">Abidîn near Bêtirrâ,</hi> thus the name of the other village is to be changed from ΑΔΑΡΩΝ to ΑΡΑΡΩΝ (for which the <hi type="italic">Cod. Vat</hi>. erroneously has ΔΡΑΡΩΝ), the modern 'Arâr.<note placement="foot">Some, in connection with this word, have erroneously thought of the city of <hi type="italic">Edre'ât</hi>, which Eusebius calls Ἀδρά in the immediately preceding article Ἀδραά, and in the art. Edraei'.</note><hi type="italic">'Abîdîn</hi>, however, lies nine miles west, and <hi type="italic">'Arâr</hi> nine miles east of <hi type="italic">'Ashtarâ</hi>. <div eID="gen8883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8884" type="x-p"/> Now, as to the second village, and its respective castle, which is mentioned in the second citation from the <hi type="italic">Onomastikon</hi>, I believe that both Euseb. and Jerome intend to say there are two villages, of which the one has the byname of the other; consequently the one is called <hi type="italic">Astarôt</hi> (<hi type="italic">Karnaim</hi>), and the other <hi type="italic">Karnaim</hi> (<hi type="italic">Astarôt</hi>). Twelve miles west of <hi type="italic">'Ashtarâ</hi> lies the Golanite village of <hi type="italic">Kornîje</hi> (קרניּה), which in old <hi type="italic">Kanêtra</hi> I have taken up in my trigonometrical measurements. <div eID="gen8884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8885" type="x-p"/> We find also a third passage in the Onomast. which belongs here; it is under Ἰαβώκ in <hi type="italic">Cod. Vat.,</hi> under Ἰδουμαία in <hi type="italic">Cod. Leid.</hi> and <hi type="italic">Vellarsi</hi>, and runs: “According to the view of a certain one (κατά τινος), this region is the land of <hi type="italic">Asitis</hi> (<hi type="italic">Ausitis</hi>), the home of Job, while according to others it is Arabia (ἡ Ἀραβία); and again, according to others, it is the Land of Sîhôn.” Whether genuine or not, this passage possesses a certain value. If it is genuine, Jerome would have left it accordingly untranslated, because he would not be responsible for its whole contents, for he not unfrequently passes over or alters statements of Eusebius where he believes himself to be better informed; but, taken exactly, he could only have rejected the views of those who seek Job’s native country on the <hi type="italic">Jabbok</hi> (if the passage belongs to the art. Ἰαβώκ) or in Edom (if it belongs to Ἰδουμαία), or in the <hi type="italic">Belkâ</hi>, the land of Sîhôn; but not the view of those who make Arabia (<hi type="italic">Batanaea</hi>) to be <hi type="italic">Ausitis</hi>, for the statement of Eusebius with reference to this point under Carnaei'm he translates faithfully. If the passage is not genuine, it at any rate gives the very early testimony of an authority distinct from Eusebius and Jerome in favour of the age of the Hauranitish tradition concerning Job, while it has only a single (κατά τινος) authority for the view of those who make Edom to be Ausitis, and even this only when the passage belongs to Ἰδουμαία. <div eID="gen8885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8886" type="x-p"/> By means of these quotations from the <hi type="italic">Onomastikon</hi>, that passage of Chrysostom (<hi type="italic">Homil. V. de Stud</hi>. §1, tom. ii. p. 59), in which it is said that many pilgrims from the end of the earth come to Arabia, in order to seek for the dunghill on which Job lay, and with rapture to kiss the ground where he suffered ( -  - ἀπὸ περάτων τῆς γῆς εἰς τῆν Ἀραβίαν τρέχοντες, ἵνα τῆν κοπρίαν ἴδωσι, καὶ θεασάμενοι καταφιλήσωσι τῆν γῆν), appears also to obtain its right local reference. This Arabia is certainly none other than that which Eusebius explains by ἣ καὶ Βαταναία, and that κοπρία or <hi type="italic">mezbele</hi> to be sought nowhere except near the <hi type="italic">Makâm Êjûb</hi>. And should there by any doubts upon the subject, ought they not to be removed by the consideration that the proud structure of the Monastery of Job, with its spring festivals mentioned above, standing like a Pharos casting its light far and wide in that age, did not allow either the Syrian Christians or the pilgrims from foreign parts to mistake the place, which tradition had rendered sacred, as the place of Job’s sufferings? <div eID="gen8886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8887" type="x-p"/> There is no monastery whose origin, according to an unimpeachable testimony, belongs to such an early date as that of the Monastery of Job. According to the chronicles of the peoples (<hi type="italic">ta'rı̂ch el - umem</hi>), or the annals of <hi type="italic">Hamze el-Isfahâni</hi> (died about 360 of the Hegira), it was built by <hi type="italic">'Amr</hi> I, the second Gefnide. Now, since the first Ghassanitish king (<hi type="italic">Gefne</hi> I) reigned forty-five years and three months, and <hi type="italic">'Amr</hi> five years, the Monastery would have been in existence about 200 a.d., if we place the beginning of the Gefnide dynasty in the time 150 a.d. Objections are raised against such an early date, because one is accustomed on good authority to assign the origin of monasteries to about the year 300 a.d. In the face of more certain historical dates, these objections must remain unheeded, for hermit and monastery life (<hi type="italic">rahbanı̂ja</hi>) existed in the country east of Jordan among the Essenes and other societies and forms of worship, even before Christianity; so that the latter, on its appearance in that part, which took place long before 200 a.d., received the monasteries as an inheritance: but certainly the chronology of the Gefnide dynasty is not reliable. <hi type="italic">Hamze</hi> fixes the duration of the dynasty at 616 years; <hi type="italic">Ibn Sa'îd</hi>,<note placement="foot">Wetzstein, Catal. Arab. MSS collected in Damascus, No. 1, p. 89.</note> in his history of the pre-Islamic Arabs, at 601 years; and to the same period extends the statement of <hi type="italic">Mejânishi</hi>,<note placement="foot">Wetzst. Catal. Arab. MSS collected in Damascus, No. 24, p. 16.</note> who, in his topography of the <hi type="italic">Ka'be</hi>, says that between the conquest of Mekka by <hi type="italic">Ta'lebe</hi> and the rule of the <hi type="italic">Kosî</hi> in this city was 500 years. On the contrary, however, <hi type="italic">Ibn Jusef</hi><note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Hamzae Isfahan. Annales</hi>, ed. Gottwald, Vorrede, p. xi.</note> informs us that this dynasty began “earlier” than 400 years before Islamism. With this statement accord all those numerous accounts, according to which the “rupture of the dyke” (<hi type="italic">sêl el - ‛arim</hi>), the supposed cause of the Jemanic emigration, took place rather more than 400 years before Islamism. If therefore, to content ourselves with an approximate calculation, we make Islamism to begin about 615 (the year of the “Mission” was 612 a.d.), and the Gefnide dynasty, with the addition of the “earlier,” 415 years previous, then the commencement of the reign of Gefne I would have been 200 a.d., and the erection of the Monastery shortly before 250. <div eID="gen8887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8888" type="x-p"/> When the tribe whose king later on built the Monastery migrated from Jemen into Syria, the Trachonitis was in the hands of a powerful race of the <hi type="italic">Kudâ'ides</hi>, which had settled there in the first century of our era, having likewise come out of Jemen, and become tributary to the Romans. This race had embraced Christianity from the natives; and some historians maintain that it permitted the <hi type="italic">Gefnides</hi> to settle and share in the possession of the country, only on the condition that they likewise should embrace Christianity. In those early times, these tribes, of course, with the new religion received the tradition of Job also from the first hand, from the Jews and the Jewish Christians, who, since the battle of the Jewish people with the Romans, will have found refuge and safety to a large extent in Petraea, and especially in the hardly accessible Trachonitis. The Nukra also, as the most favoured region of Syria and Palestina, will have had its native population, among which, in spite of the frequent massacres of Syrians and Jews, there will have been many Jews. Perhaps, moreover, the protection of the new Jemanic population of Hauran again attracted Jewish settlers thither: Nawâ<note placement="foot">If <hi type="italic">Nawâ</hi> is not also of Jewish origin, its name is nevertheless the old Semitic נוה, “a dwelling” (<reference osisRef="Job.5.3">Job 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.5.24">Job 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.8.6">Job 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.15">Job 18:15</reference>), and not, as <hi type="italic">Jâkût</hi> supposes, the collective form of <hi type="italic">nawât</hi>, “the kernel of a date.”</note> at least is a place well known in the Talmud and Midrash, which is mentioned, as a city inhabited by the Jews among those who are not Jews, and as the birth-place of several eminent teachers.<note placement="foot">No less than three renowned teachers from <hi type="italic">Nawâ</hi> appear in the Talmud and Midrash: ר שׁילא דנוה, <hi type="italic">Schila</hi> of <hi type="italic">Nawa</hi> (<hi type="italic">jer. Sabbath</hi> cap. ii., <hi type="italic">Wajikra rabba</hi> cap. xxxiv., <hi type="italic">Midrasch Ruth</hi> on ii. 19 <hi type="italic">a</hi>), ר פלטיא דנוה (<hi type="italic">Midr. Koheleth</hi> on i. 4 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) and ר שׁאול דנוה (<hi type="italic">ib.</hi> on xii. 9 <hi type="italic">a</hi>). נוה is mentioned as an enemy of the neighbouring town of חלמיש in <hi type="italic">Wajikra rabba</hi> c. xxiii., <hi type="italic">Midr. Echa</hi> on i. 17 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Midr. Schir</hi> on ii. 1. - Del.</note> <div eID="gen8888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8889" type="x-p"/> Moreover, in Syria the veneration of a spot consecrated by religious tradition is independent of its being at the time inhabited or desolate. The supposed tombs of Aaron near <hi type="italic">Petra</hi>, of Hud near <hi type="italic">Gerash</hi>, of Jethro (<hi type="italic">Su'êb</hi>) in the valley of <hi type="italic">Nimrîn</hi>, of Ezekiel in <hi type="italic">Melîhat Hiskîn</hi>, of Elisha on the <hi type="italic">el-Jesha'</hi> mountains, and many other <hi type="italic">mezâre</hi> (tombs of the holy, to which pilgrims resort), are frequently one or more days’ journey distant from inhabited places, and yet they are carefully tended. They are preserved from decay and neglect by vows, by the spring processions, and especially by the piety of the Beduins, who frequently deposit articles of value near the <hi type="italic">mezâre</hi>, as property entrusted to the care of the saint. The Makâm of Job may also have been such a consecrated spot many centuries before the erection of the Monastery, and perhaps not merely to the Jews, but also to the Aramaean and Arab population. The superstitious veneration of such places is not confined among the Semites to a particular religious sect, but is the common heritage of the whole race; and the tradition of Job in particular was, originally, certainly not Israelitish, but Aramaean. <div eID="gen8889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8890" type="x-p"/> Job is not mentioned in the writings of Josephus, but we do find there a remarkable passage concerning Job’s native country, the land of the Usites, viz., <hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> i. 6: “<hi type="italic">Aram</hi>, from whom come the <hi type="italic">Aramaeans,</hi> called by the Greeks <hi type="italic">Syrians</hi>, had four sons, of whom the first was named Οὔσης, and possessed <hi type="italic">Trachonitis</hi> and <hi type="italic">Damascus</hi>.” The first of these two, Trachonitis, has usually been overlooked here, and attention has been fixed only on Damascus. The word <hi type="italic">el-Ghûta</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - gûṭt</hi>), the proper name of the garden and orchard district around Damascus, has been thought to be connected in sound with 'Us, and they have been treated as identical: this is, however, impossible even in philological grounds. <hi type="italic">Ghûta</hi> would certainly be written עוּטה in Hebrew, because this language has no sign for the sound <hi type="italic">Gh</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">g</hi>); but Josephus, who wrote in Greek, ought then to have said Γούσης, not Οὔσης, just as he, and the lxx before him and Eusebius after him, render the city עזה by Γάζα, the mountain עיבל by Γαιβάλ, the village עי by Γαΐ́, etc. In the same manner the lxx ought to have spoken of a Γαυσῖτις, not Αὐσῖτις, if this were the case. Proper names, also, always receive too definite and lasting an impress for their consonants, as ץ and ט, to be easily interchanged, although this is possible with the roots of verbs. Moreover, if the word עוץ had had the consonant ץ (Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍ</hi>), Josephus must have reproduced it with τ or θ, not with s, in accordance with the pronunciation (especially if he had intended to identify עוץ and <hi type="italic">Ghûta</hi>). And we see from Ptolemy and Strabo, and likewise from the Greek mode of transcribing the Semitic proper names in the Haurânite inscriptions of the Roman period, e.g., Μάθιος and Νάταρος for Arab. <hi type="italic">mâḍâ</hi> and <hi type="italic">nḍr</hi>, that in the time of Josephus the sound of ץ had already been divided into Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣ</hi> and <hi type="italic">ḍ</hi>; comp. <hi type="italic">Abhandl. der Berlin. Acad. d. Wissenschaft,</hi> 1863, S. 356f. Hence it is that Josephus manifestly speaks only of one progenitor Οὔσης, therefore of one tribe; while the word <hi type="italic">Ghûta</hi>, often as a synonym of <hi type="italic">buq'a</hi> (בקעה), denotes a low well-watered country enclosed by mountains, and in this appellative signification occurs as the proper name of several localities in the <hi type="italic">most widely separated parts of Arabia</hi> (comp. <hi type="italic">Jâkût, sub voce</hi>), which could not be the case if it had been = ארץ עוץ.<note placement="foot">On the name 'Us, as the name of men and people, may be compared the proper names 'As and <hi type="italic">'Aus</hi>, together with the diminutive <hi type="italic">'Owês</hi>, taken from the genealogies of the Arabs, since the Old Testament is wanting in words formed from the root עוץ, and none of those so named was a Hebrew. In Hebr. they might be sounded עוץ, and signify the “strong one,” for the verbal stems Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ṣṣ , ‛wṣ , ‛ṣy</hi> (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ṣb , ‛ṣr , ‛ṣm ,</hi> and others) have the signif. “to be compressed, firm, to resist.”</note> <div eID="gen8890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8891" type="x-p"/> The word <hi type="italic">Ausitis</hi> used by the lxx also has no formation corresponding to the word <hi type="italic">Ghûta</hi>, but shows its connection with עוּץ ארץ by the termination; while the word <hi type="italic">Ghûta</hi> rendered in Greek is Gouthata' (in Theophanes Byzant. Gouthatha'), in analogy e.g., with the form Cheblatha' for <hi type="italic">Ribla</hi> (Jos. <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. x. 11).<note placement="foot">On this word-formation comp. <hi type="italic">Reisebericht</hi>, S. 76.</note> <div eID="gen8891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8892" type="x-p"/> But why are we obliged to think only of Damascus, since Josephus makes <hi type="italic">Trachonitis</hi> also to belong to the land of the <hi type="italic">Usites?</hi> If we take this word in its most limited signification, it is (apart from the eastern <hi type="italic">Trachon</hi>) that lava plateau, about forty miles long and about twenty-eight broad, which is called the <hi type="italic">Legâ</hi> in the present day. This is so certain, that one is not obliged first of all to recall the well-known inscription of the temple of <hi type="italic">Mismia</hi>, which calls this city situated in the Legâ, Μητροκώμη τοῦ Τράχωνος. From the western border of this <hi type="italic">Trachon</hi>, however, the Monastery of Job is not ten miles distant, therefore by no means outside the radius that was at all times tributary to the Trachonites (<hi type="italic">Arab el-wa'r</hi>), a people unassailable in their habitations in the clefts of the rocks.<note placement="foot">Comp. Jos. <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. xv. 10, 3; <hi type="italic">Zeitschr. für allg. Erdkunde,</hi> New Series, xiii. 213.</note> <div eID="gen8892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8893" type="x-p"/> According to this, the statement of Josephus would at least not stand in open contradiction to the Hauranitish tradition of Job. But we go further and maintain that the Monastery of Job lies exactly in the centre of <hi type="italic">Trachonitis</hi>. This word has, viz., in Josephus and others, a double signification - a more limited and a wider one. It has the more limited where, together with <hi type="italic">Auranitis, Batanaea, Gamalitica,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Gaulonitis</hi>, it denotes the separate provinces of the ancient kingdom of <hi type="italic">Basan</hi>. Then it signifies the <hi type="italic">Trachonitis</hi> kat' exochee'n, i.e., the wildest portion of the volcanic district, viz., the <hi type="italic">Legâ</hi>, the <hi type="italic">Haurân</hi> mountain range, the <hi type="italic">Safâ</hi> and <hi type="italic">Harra</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Râgil</hi>. On the other hand, it has the wider signification when it stands alone; then it embraces the whole volcanic region of Middle Syria, therefore with the more limited Trachonitis the remaining provinces of Basan, but with the exception, as it seems, of the no longer volcanic <hi type="italic">Galadine</hi> (North Gilead). In this sense, therefore, as a geographical notion, Trachonitis is almost synonymous with Basan. <div eID="gen8893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8894" type="x-p"/> Since it is to the interest of this investigation to make the assertion advanced sure against every objection, we will not withhold the passages in support of it. Josephus says, <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. xv. 10, 3, the district of <hi type="italic">Hûle</hi> (Οὐλαθά) lies between Galilee and Trachonitis. He might have said more accurately, “between Galilee and Gaulonitis,” but he wished to express that the great basaltic region begins on the eastern boundary of the <hi type="italic">Hûle</hi>. The word Trachonitis has therefore the <hi type="italic">wider</hi> signification. In like manner, in <hi type="italic">Bell</hi>. iii. 10 it is said the lake of <hi type="italic">Phiala</hi> lies 120 stadia east of Paneion (<hi type="italic">Bâniâs</hi>) on the way to the Trachonitis. True, the Phiala is a crater, and therefore itself belongs to Trachonitis, but between it and Bâniâs the lava alternates with the chalk formation of the Hermôn, whereas to the south and east of the Phiala it is everywhere exclusively volcanic; Trachonitis has therefore here also the <hi type="italic">wider</hi> signification. <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. xvii. 2, it is said Herod had the castle of Βαθύρα built in Batanaea (here, as often in Josephus, in the signification of Basan), in order to protect the Jews who travel from Babylon (<hi type="italic">viâ</hi> Damascus) to Jerusalem against the Trachonite robbers. Now, since this castle and village (the <hi type="italic">Bêtirrâ</hi> mentioned already), which is situated in the district of <hi type="italic">Gamalitica</hi> on an important ford of the <hi type="italic">Muchêbi</hi> gorge between <hi type="italic">'Abidin</hi> and <hi type="italic">Sebbûte</hi>, could not be any protection against the robbers of Trachonitis in the more limited sense, but only against those of Golan, it is manifest that by the Trachonites are meant the robbers of Trachonitis in the <hi type="italic">wider</hi> sense. Aurelius Victor (<hi type="italic">De Hist. Caes</hi>. xxvii.) calls the Emperor M. Julius Philippus, born in <hi type="italic">Bosrâ</hi>, the metropolis of Auranitis, quite correctly <hi type="italic">Arabs Trachonites;</hi> because the plain of Hauran, in which Bosra is situated, is also of a basaltic formation, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> is a part of the Trachonitis. <div eID="gen8894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8895" type="x-p"/> The passage of Luke’s Gospel, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.1">Luk 3:1</reference>, where it says Herod tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, also belongs here. That Philip possessed not perhaps merely the Trachonitis (similar to a province assigned to a man as banishment rather than for administration, producing little or no revenue) in the more <hi type="italic">limited</hi> sense, but the whole Basanitis, is shown by Josephus, who informs us, <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. xvii. 11, 4 and freq., that he possessed Batanaea (in the more restricted sense, therefore the fruitful, densely populated, profitable Nukra), with Auranitis, Trachonitis, etc. We must therefore suppose that in the words τῆς Ἰτουραίας καὶ Τραχωνίτιδος χώρας in Luke, one district is meant, which by Ἰτουραίας is mentioned according to the marauding portion of its population, and by Trachooni'tidos more generally, according to its trachonitic formation.<note placement="foot">Eusebius in his <hi type="italic">Onomast</hi>. also correctly identifies the two words, at one time under Ἰτουραία, and the other time under Τραχωνῖτις. After what we have said elsewhere (<hi type="italic">Reisebericht</hi>, S. 91ff.) on the subject, surely no one will again maintain that the peaceful villages of the plain of Gêdûr were the abodes of the Ituraeans, the wildest of all people (Cic. <hi type="italic">Phil</hi>. ii. 11; Strabo, xvi. 2). Their principal hiding-places will have been the Trachonitis in the more restricted sense, but one may seek them also on the wooded mountains of <hi type="italic">Gôlân</hi> and in the gorges of the <hi type="italic">Makran</hi>. That Ptolemy and Josephus speak only of the Trachonites and never of the Ituraeans (in the passage <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. xiii. 11, 3, Ἰδουμαία is to be read instead of Ἰτουραία), and Strabo, on the other hand, speaks only of the latter, favours the identity of the two; of like import is the circumstance, that Pliny (<hi type="italic">H. N.</hi> v. 23) makes the inhabitants of the region of Baetarra (Bêtirrâ) Ituraeans, and Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. xvii. 2) Trachonites. But in spite of the identity of the words <hi type="italic">Trachonitis</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ituraea</hi>, one must not at the same time overlook the following distinction. If the Trachonites are called after the country, it must be the description of all the inhabitants of the country, whereas the Ituraeans, if they gave the name to the country, are not necessarily its exclusive population. The whole of the district of which we speak has a twofold population in keeping with its double character (rugged rock and fruitful plain), viz., cattle-rearing freebooters in the clefts of the rocks, and peaceful husbandmen in the plain; the former dwelling in hair tents (of old also in caves), the latter in stone houses; the former forming the large majority, the latter the minority of the population of the district. If writers speak of the <hi type="italic">Ituraeans</hi>, they mean exclusively that marauding race that hates husbandry; but if they speak of the <hi type="italic">Trachonites</hi>, the connection must determine, whether they speak of both classes of the population, or only of the marauding Trachonites (the Ituraeans), or of the husbandmen of the plain (of the provinces of <hi type="italic">Batanaea</hi> and <hi type="italic">Auranitis</hi>). The latter are rarely intended, since the peaceful peasant rarely furnishes material for the historian.</note> <div eID="gen8895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8896" type="x-p"/> Ioannes Malalas (<hi type="italic">Chronogr. ed. Dindorf,</hi> p. 236), who, as a Syrian born, ought to be well acquainted with the native usage of the language, hence calls Antipas, as a perfectly adequate term, only toparch of Trachonitis; and if, according to his statement (p. 237), the official title of this Herod was the following: Σεβαστὸς Ἡρώδης τοπάρχης καὶ θεσμοδότης Ἰουδαίων τε καὶ Ἑλλήνων, Βασιλεὺς τῆς Τραχωνίτιδος, it is self-evident that “king of Trachonitis” here is synonymous with king of Basan. In perfect harmony with this, Pliny says (<hi type="italic">H. N.</hi> v. 18) that the ten cities of Decapolis lay within the extensive tetrarchies of Trachonitis, which are divided into separate kingdoms. Undoubtedly Pliny adds to these tetrarchies of Trachonitis in the wider sense, which are already known to us, <hi type="italic">Galadine</hi> also, which indeed belonged also the pre-Mosaic <hi type="italic">Basan</hi>, but at the time of Josephus is mostly reckoned to <hi type="italic">Peraea</hi> (in the more limited sense). <div eID="gen8896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8897" type="x-p"/> On the ground of this evidence, therefore, the land of the Usites of Josephus, with the exception of the Damascene portion, was Trachonitis in the wider sense; and since the Makâm Êjûb is in the central point of this country, this statement accords most exactly with the Syrian tradition. It is clear that the latter remains untouched by the extension of the geographical notion in Josephus, for without knowing anything more of a “land of the Usites,” it describes only a portion of the same as the “native country of Job;” and again, Josephus had no occasion to speak of Job in his commentary on the genealogies, therefore also none to speak of his special home within the land of the Usites. Eusebius, on the other hand, in his <hi type="italic">De Originibus</hi> (ix. 2, 4), refers to this home, and says, therefore limiting Josephus’ definition: <hi type="italic">Hus, Traconitidis conditor, inter Palaestinam et Coelesyriam tenuit imperium; unde fuit Iob</hi>. <div eID="gen8897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8898" type="x-p"/> With this evidence of agreement between two totally independent witnesses, viz., the Syrian tradition and Josephus, the testimony of the latter in particular has an enhanced value; for, although connected with the Bible, it nevertheless avails as extra-biblical testimony concerning the Usites, it comes from an age when one might still have the historical fact from the seat of the race, and from an authority of the highest order. True, Josephus is not free from disfigurements, where he has the opportunity of magnifying his people, himself, or his Roman patrons, and of depreciating an enemy; but here he had to do with nothing more than the statement of the residence of a people; and since the word Ou'sees also has no similarity in sound with the words <hi type="italic">Damascus</hi> and <hi type="italic">Trachonitis</hi>, that might make a combination with them plausible, we may surely have before us a reliable historical notice here, or at least a tradition which was then general (and therefore also for us important), while we may doubt this in connection with other parts of the genealogies, where Josephus seems only to catch at that which is similar in sound as furnishing an explanation. <div eID="gen8898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8899" type="x-p"/> But that which might injure the authority of Josephus is the contradiction in which it seems to stand to a far older statement concerning <hi type="italic">Ausitis</hi>, viz., the recognised postscript of the lxx to the book of Job, which makes Job to be the Edomitish king Jobab. The identification, it may be said, can however only have been possible because <hi type="italic">Ausitis</hi> was in or near Edom. But the necessity of this inference must be disputed. It is indeed unmistakeable that that postscript is nothing more than a combination of the Jews beyond Palestine (probably Egytpio-Hellenistic), formed, perhaps, long before the lxx, - such a vagary as many similar ones in the Talmud and Midrash. From the similarity in sound of Ἰωβάβ with Ἰώβ, and the similarity in name of Ζαρά, the father of <hi type="italic">Jobab</hi>, with a son of Re'ûël and grandson of Esau (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.13">Gen 36:13</reference>), Job’s descent from Esau has been inferred. That Esau’s first-born was called <hi type="italic">Elîphaz</hi> and his son <hi type="italic">Temân</hi>, seemed to confirm this combination, since (in accordance with the custom<note placement="foot">From this custom, which is called the grandfather’s “living again,” the habit, singular to us, of a father calling his son <hi type="italic">jâ abı̂</hi>, “my father!” or <hi type="italic">jâ bêjı̂</hi>, “my little father,” as an endearing form of address, is explained.</note> of naming the grandson as a rule after his grandfather) <hi type="italic">Elîphaz</hi> the Temanite might be regarded as grandson of that <hi type="italic">Elîphaz</hi>, therefore like Job as great-grandson of Esau and πέμπτος ἀπὸ Ἀβραάμ. The apparent and certainly designed advantages of this combination were: that Job, who had no pedigree, and therefore was to be thought of as a non-Israelite, was brought into the nearest possible blood-relationship to the people of God, and that, by laying the scene in the time of the patriarchs, all questions which the want of a Mosaic colouring to the book of Job might excite would be met. Now, even if the abode of Job were transferred from the land of <hi type="italic">'Us</hi> to Edom, it would be only the consequence of his combination with <hi type="italic">Jobab</hi>, and, just as worthless as this latter itself, might lead no one astray. But it does not seem to have gone so far; it is even worthy of observation, that מבצרה (from <hi type="italic">Bosra</hi>, the Edomite city),<note placement="foot">It need hardly be mentioned that one is not to think of the Hauranitish <hi type="italic">Bosrâ</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">bṣrâ</hi>), since this name of a city only came into use some centuries after Christ.</note> being attached to the misunderstood υἱὸς Ζαρά ἐκ Βοσόῤῥας, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.33">Gen 36:33</reference>, is reproduced in the lxx by μητρὸς Βοσόῤῥας, as also that Job’s wife is not called an Edomitess, but a γυνὴ Ἀράβισσα. And it appears still far more important, that Ausitis lies ἐν τοῖς ὁρίοις τῆς Ἰδουμαίας καὶ Ἀραβίας, so far as the central point of Ἰδουμαία is removed by the addition καὶ τῆς Ἀραβίας, and Job’s abode is certainly removed from the heart of Idumaea. The <hi type="italic">Cod. Alex.</hi> exchanges that statement of the place, even in a special additional clause, for ἐπὶ τῶν ὁρίων τοῦ Εὐφράτου, therefore transfers Ausitis to the vicinity of the Euphrates, and calls the father of Jobab (= Job) Ζαρὲθ ἐξ ἀνατολῶν ἡλίου (מבני קדם). Nevertheless we attach no importance to this variation of the text, but rather offer the suggestion that the postscript gives prominence to the observation: οὗτος (viz., Ἰώβ) ἑρμεενεύεται ἐκ τῆς Συριακῆς βίβλου.<note placement="foot">It is indeed possible that the Hebrew text is meant here, for Philo usually calls the Hebrew Χαλδαΐστί, and the Talmud describes the Jewish country-dialect as סורסי; it is possible, and even more probable, that it is a Syrian, i.e., Aramaean Targum - but not less possible that it is a Syrian original document. According to Malalas (<hi type="italic">ed. Dindorf</hi>, p. 12), Origen understands ἐκ τῆς Συριακῆς βίβλου elsewhere of a Hebrew original, but in <hi type="italic">c. Celsum</hi> iii. 6 he describes the Hebrew language in relation to the Syriac and Phoenician as ἑτέρα παρ ̓ ἀμθοτέρας, and the Homilies on Job in <hi type="italic">Opp. Origenis, ed. Delaure,</hi> ii. 851, say: <hi type="italic">Beati Iob scriptura primum quidem in Arabia Syriace scripta, ubi et habitabat</hi>. - Del.</note> <div eID="gen8899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8900" type="x-p"/> If we compare the postscript of the lxx with the legend of Islam, we find in both the Esauitish genealogy of Job; the genealogy of the legend is: <hi type="italic">Êjûb ibn Zârih</hi> (זרח) <hi type="italic">ibn Reû'îl ibn el-'Ais ibn Ishâk ibn Ibrâhîm;</hi> and we may suppose that it is borrowed directly from the lxx, and that it reached Arabia and Mekka even in the pre-Islamic times by means of the (Arabian) Christians east of Jordan, who had the Old Testament only in the Greek translation. Even the Arabic orthography of the biblical proper names, which can be explained only on the supposition of their transfer from the Greek, is in favour of this mode of the transmission of the Christian religion and its legends to the people of the <hi type="italic">Higaz</hi>. Certainly there can be no doubt as to an historical connection between the postscript and the legend, and therefore it would be strange if they did not accord respecting the home of Job. The progenitor <hi type="italic">el-'Ais</hi> (עיץ), in the genealogy of the legend, is also a remarkable counterpart to the Ausitis ἐν τοῖς ὁρίοις τῆς Ἰδουμ. καὶ Ἀρ., for it is a blending of עשׂו and עוּץ, and it has to solve the difficult problem, as to how Job can be at the same time an <hi type="italic">Usite</hi> and an <hi type="italic">Esauite;</hi> for that Job as an Aisite no longer belongs to Idumaea, but to the district of the more northern Aramaeans, is shown e.g., from the following passage in <hi type="italic">Mugîr ed-dîn's</hi> History of Jerusalem: “Job belonged to the people of the Romans (i.e., the <hi type="italic">Aisites</hi>),<note placement="foot">We will spare ourselves the ungrateful task of an inquiry into the origin of this <hi type="italic">'Ais</hi> and his Protean nature. Biblical passages like <reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">Lam 4:21</reference>, or those in which the readings ארם and אדום are doubtful, or the erroneous supposition (Jos. <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. viii. 7) that the <hi type="italic">Ben-Hadad</hi> dynasty in Damascus is of Edomitish origin, may have contributed to his rise. Moreover, he is altogether one and the same with the <hi type="italic">Edom</hi> of the Jerish tradition: he is called the father of <hi type="italic">Rûm, Asfar, Sôfar, Sîfûn</hi> (מלך חצפון), and <hi type="italic">Nidr</hi> (<hi type="italic">Hamz. Isfah. Ann</hi>. p. 79, l. 18, read Arab. <hi type="italic">ndr</hi> for <hi type="italic">ntsr</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Zeitschr. d. d. m. Gesellsch</hi>. ii. 239, 3, 6, read <hi type="italic">ennidr </hi>for <hi type="italic">ennefer</hi>), i.e., of the Messiah of the Christians (according to <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa 11:1</reference>)</note> for he sprang from <hi type="italic">el-'Ais</hi>, and the Damascene province of <hi type="italic">Batanaea</hi> was his property.” <div eID="gen8900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8901" type="x-p"/> The κοπρία of the lxx, at <reference osisRef="Job.2.8">Job 2:8</reference>, leads to the same result; that it is also found again as <hi type="italic">mezbele</hi> in the later legend, is a further proof how thoroughly this accords with the lxx, and how it has understood its statement of the position of <hi type="italic">Ausitis</hi>. It may also be maintained here, that it was only possible to translate the words בתוך־חאפר by ἐπὶ τῆς κοπρίας ἔξω τῆς πόλεως when “heap of ashes” and “dunghill” were synonymous notions. This, however, is the case only in Hauran, where the dung, as being useless for agricultural purposes, is burnt from time to time in an appointed place before the town (vid., p. 573),<note placement="foot">Comp. p. 576, note, of the foregoing Commentary. The Arabic version of Walton’s Polyglot translates after the Peschito in accordance with the Hebr. text: “on the ashes (<hi type="italic">er - remâd</hi>),” whereas the Arabic translation, of which Tischendorf brought back fifteen leaves with him from the East, and which Fleischer, in the <hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenl. Zeitschr.</hi> 1864, S. 288ff., has first described as an important memorial in reference to the history of MSS, translates after the <hi type="italic">Hexapla</hi> in accordance with the lxx: “on the dunghill (<hi type="italic">mezbele</hi>) outside the city.”-Del.</note> while in every other part of Syria it is as valuable and as much stored up as among us. If the lxx accordingly placed the kopri'a of Job in Hauran, it could hardly represent <hi type="italic">Ausitis</hi> as <hi type="italic">Edom</hi>. <div eID="gen8901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8902" type="x-p"/> But how has the Ausitis of the lxx been transferred hither? Certainly not as the “land of '<hi type="italic">Us</hi>” (in the sense of the land of <hi type="italic">Basan</hi>, land of <hi type="italic">Haurân</hi>), for without wasting a word about it, there has never been such an one in the country east of the Jordan: but as “the land of the Usites” in the sense of the <hi type="italic">Arabic diâr 'Us</hi> (dwelling-place of the Usites) or <hi type="italic">ard benî 'Us</hi>. A land receives designations of this kind with the settlement of a people in it; they run parallel with the proper name of the country, and in the rule vanish again with that people. These designations belong, indeed, to the geography of the whole earth, but nowhere have they preserved their natural character of transitoriness more faithfully than in the lands where the Semitic tongue is spoken. It is this that makes the geographical knowledge of these countries so extremely difficult to us, because we frequently take them to be the names of the countries, which they are not, and which - so far as they always involve a geological definition of the regions named - can never be displaced and competently substituted by them. In this sense the <hi type="italic">land of the Usites</hi> might, at the time of the decay of both Israelitish kingdoms, when the ארם דמשׂק possessed the whole of Peraea, very easily extend from the borders of Edom to the gates of Damascus, and even further northwards, if the Aramaean race of <hi type="italic">'Us</hi> numbered many or populous tribes (as it appears to be indicated in כל מלכי ארץ העוץ, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.20">Jer 25:20</reference>), in perfect analogy with the tribe of <hi type="italic">Ghassân</hi>, which during five hundred years occupied the country from the Aelanitic Gulf to the region of <hi type="italic">Tedmor</hi>, at one time settling down, at another leading a nomadic life, and Hauran was the centre of its power. By such a rendering the Ἀραβία of the postscript would not be different from the later <hi type="italic">provincia Arabiae</hi>, of which the capital was the Trachonitish <hi type="italic">Bostra</hi>, while is was bounded on the south end of the Dead Sea by Edom (<hi type="italic">Palaestine tertia</hi>). <div eID="gen8902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8903" type="x-p"/> But should any one feel a difficulty in freeing himself from the idea that <hi type="italic">Ausitis</hi> is to be sought only in the <hi type="italic">Ard el-Hâlât</hi> east of <hi type="italic">Ma'ân</hi>, he must consider that the author of the book of Job could not, like that legend which places the miraculous city of <hi type="italic">Iram</hi> in the country of quicksands, transfer the cornfields of his hero to the desert; for there, with the exception of smaller patches of land capable of culture, which we may not bring into account, there is by no means to be found that husbandman’s Eldorado, where a single husbandman might find tillage for five hundred (<reference osisRef="Job.1.3">Job 1:3</reference>), yea, for a thousand (<reference osisRef="Job.42.12">Job 42:12</reference>) yoke of oxen. Such numbers as these are not to be depreciated; for in connection with the primitive agriculture in Syria and Palestine, - which renders a four years’ alternation of crops necessary, so that the fields must be divided into so many portions (called in Hauran <hi type="italic">wâgihât</hi>, and around Damascus <hi type="italic">auguh</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">'wjh</hi>), from which only one portion is used annually, and the rest left fallow (<hi type="italic">bûr</hi>), - Job required several square miles of tillage for the employment of his oxen. It is all the same in this respect whether the book of Job is a history or poem: in no case could the <hi type="italic">Ausitis</hi> be a country, the notorious sterility of which would make the statement of the poet ridiculous. <div eID="gen8903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8904" type="x-p"/> Our limited space does not admit of our proving the worth which we must acknowledge to the tradition, by illustrating those passages of the Old Testament scriptures which have reference to עוץ and ארץ עוץ. But to any one, who, following the hints they give, wishes again to pursue the investigations, elsewhere useless, concerning the position of the land of the Usites, we might indicate: (1) that עוץ the first-born of Aram (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.23">Gen 10:23</reference>) is the tribe sought, while two others of this name - a Nahorite, <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job 22:21</reference>, and a Horite, <reference osisRef="Job.36.28">Job 36:28</reference> - may be left out of consideration; the former because the twelve sons of Nahor need not be progenitors of tribes, and the latter because he belongs to a tribe exterminated by the Edomites in accordance with <reference osisRef="Deut.2.12">Deu 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.22">Deu 2:22</reference> : (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.2">2</reference>) that ארץ העוץ, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.20">Jer 25:20</reference>, is expressly distinguished from אדום in the <reference osisRef="Jer.25.21">Jer 25:21</reference>, and - if one compares the round of the cup of punishment, Jer. 25, with the detailed prophecies which follow in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.1">Jer 46:1</reference>, to which it is a prooemium that has been removed from its place - corresponds to דמשׂק (with <hi type="italic">Hamât</hi> and <hi type="italic">Arpad</hi>), <reference osisRef="Jer.49.23">Jer 49:23</reference> : (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">3</reference>) that therefore <reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">Lam 4:21</reference>, where יושׁבת בארץ עוץ would be devoid of purpose if it described the proper habitable land of Edom, must describe a district extending over that, in which the Edomites had established themselves in consequence of Assyria having led away captive the Israelitish and Aramaean population of the East Jordanic country and Coele-Syria. In connection with <reference osisRef="Jer.25.20">Jer 25:20</reference> one must not avoid the question whether עוץ is the name of the ארם דמשׂק that has been missed. Here the migration of the Damascene Aramaeans from <hi type="italic">Kîr</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.7">Amo 9:7</reference>) ought to be considered, the value of the Armenian accounts concerning the original abode of the Usites tested, what is erroneous in the combination of קיר with the river <hi type="italic">Kur</hi> shown and well considered, and in what relations both as to time and events that migration might have stood to the overrunning of Middle Syria by the Aramaean <hi type="italic">Sôbaean</hi> tribes (from Mesopotamia) under Hadad-ezer, and to the seizure and possession of the city of Damascus by Rezon the Sôbaean? Finally, one more tradition might be compared, to which some value may perhaps be attached, because it is favoured by the stone monuments, whose testimony we are not accustomed otherwise to despise in Palestine and Syria. The eastern portal of the mosque of <hi type="italic">Benî Umêja</hi> in Damascus, probably of the very temple, the altar of which king Ahaz caused to be copied (2Ki 16:10), is called <hi type="italic">Gêrûn</hi> or the Gerun gate: the portal in its present form belongs to the Byzantine or Roman period. And before this gate is the <hi type="italic">Gêrûnîje</hi>, a spacious, vaulted structure, mostly very old, which has been used since the Mussulman occupation of the city as a <hi type="italic">mêda'a</hi>, i.e., a place for religious ablutions. The topographical writings on Damascus trace these two names back to a <hi type="italic">Gêrûn ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ad ibn 'Aus</hi> (עוץ) <hi type="italic">ibn Iram</hi> (ארם) <hi type="italic">ibn Sâm</hi> (שׁם) <hi type="italic">ibn Nûh</hi> (נוח), who settled in Damascus in the time of Solomon (one version of the tradition identifies him with <hi type="italic">Hadad</hi>, Jos. <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. viii. 7), and built in the middle of the city a castle named after him, in which a temple to the planet (<hi type="italic">kôkeb</hi>) <hi type="italic">Mushteri</hi>, the guardian-god of the city, has been erected. That this temple, which, as is well known, under Theodosius, at the same time with the temple of the sun at Ba'lbek, passed over to the Christians, was actually surrounded with a strong, fortified wall, is capable of proof even in the present day. In this tradition, which has assumed various forms, a more genuine counterpart of the biblical עוץ appears than that <hi type="italic">'Ais</hi> which we have characterized above as an invention of the schools, viz., an <hi type="italic">'Aus</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">‛wṣ</hi>), father of the Adite-tribe which is said to have settled in the Damascene district under that <hi type="italic">Gêrûn</hi>, and also ancestor of the prophet <hi type="italic">Hûd</hi>, lost to the tradition, whose <hi type="italic">makâm</hi> on the mountains of <hi type="italic">Suêt</hi> rises far above <hi type="italic">Gerash</hi> a city of pillars, this true <hi type="italic">Iram dhât el-'imâd</hi>, the valley of the Jabbok and the <hi type="italic">Sawâd</hi> of Gilead. <div eID="gen8904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8905" type="x-p"/> It is with good reason that we have hitherto omitted to mention the Αἰσῖται of Ptolemy v. 18 (19). The Codd have both Αἰσεῖται and Αἰσῖται; different Semitic forms (e.g., the name of the Arab. <hi type="italic">bny hays</hi>, which, according to Jâkût, once dwelt in the <hi type="italic">Harra</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Ragil</hi>) may lie at the basis of this name, only not the form עוּץ, which ought to be Οὐσῖται, or at least Αὐσῖται (which no Cod. reads). As to the abodes of the Αἰσῖται, Ptolemy distributes them under nine greater races or groups of races, which in his time inhabited the Syrian steppe. Three of these had their settlements in the eastern half of the Syrian steppe towards the Euphrates of on its western banks: the Καυχαβηνοί in the north, the Αἰσῖται in the middle, and the Ὀρχηνοί in the south. According to this the Αἰσῖται would have been about between <hi type="italic">Hît</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kûfa</hi>, or in that district which is called by the natives <hi type="italic">Ard el-Wudjan</hi>, and in which just that race of the Chaldaeans might have dwelt that plundered Job’s camels. There we are certainly not to seek the scene of the drama of Job; and if the Edomites were dispersed there (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">Lam 4:21</reference>), they were not to be envied on account of their fortune.
